insights.title: Rain is more than crops can use
insights.body: Rain exceeds crop water demand by about 1115 mm a year. Waterlogging and runoff are bigger risks than drought.

insights.title: Fields are greenest in May, barest in September
insights.body: Satellite greenness of the farmland here peaks at 0.67 and drops to 0.57 (0 = bare, 1 = dense crop). The low months are when soil is most exposed to rain and wind.

insights.title: Best-matched crops for this area
insights.body: Oil palm, Rubber and Cashew score highest on climate, water and soil fit.

outlook.method: Theil-Sen trend + Mann-Kendall test on 2001-2024 yearly data, extended to 2035 with an 80% prediction range. Where there is no clear trend, the 2001-2024 average is projected. Statistical extrapolation, not a climate-model forecast.

consequences.headline: Dry spells stretching to about 22 days
consequences.detail: The longest run without rain is growing from about 15 days. Seedlings sown on the first rains, and crops in flower, can die in a long gap.
consequences.action: Wait until the rains are steady before sowing; choose short, drought-tolerant varieties.

consequences.headline: In a dry year, rain can drop to about 1,992 mm
consequences.detail: That is 18% below the 2,423 mm average; about 1 year in 10 is this dry or worse.
consequences.action: Keep a drought-tolerant crop in the plan as insurance.

consequences.headline: +0.6 °C warmer on average by 2035
consequences.detail: The yearly average moves from 26.7 °C to about 27.3 °C. Most recommended crops stay inside their temperature range.
consequences.action: Watch heat stress in cool-climate crops; earlier sowing helps.
